World.title: Azerbaijani journalists tour Sea Breeze Uzbekistan complex (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. As part of a press tour organized for Azerbaijani media representatives visiting Uzbekistan, journalists visited the “Sea Breeze Uzbekistan” resort and residential complex located on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir.

Twenty representatives from Azerbaijan’s leading media outlets are participating in the press tour. Among the participants is Emin Aliyev, editor-in-chief of the Trend International News Agency.

“Sea Breeze Uzbekistan” is a new resort and residential development located about 80 kilometers from Tashkent, spanning 527 hectares with a 7-kilometer shoreline. Planned for completion in phases between 2025 and 2035, the project will include villas, hotels, beaches, sports facilities, restaurants, leisure and wellness areas, and a boulevard.

The media representatives were also briefed on the “White Villas” and “White Residences” projects, designed to blend into Charvak’s natural landscape and offer panoramic views of the reservoir.

Mikhail Namazov, Head of Strategic Development at “Sea Breeze,” said the project is in its early stages, with landscaping already underway. He noted that the development aims to create an international-standard resort while preserving the area’s natural environment.

Namazov emphasized that the project prioritizes environmental sustainability and adapts “Sea Breeze’s” successful concepts in Azerbaijan to Charvak’s natural landscape. The resort will feature pools, restaurants, beach clubs, and entertainment facilities, hosting concerts, festivals, and sports and cultural events, he added.

“Sea Breeze Uzbekistan” is “Agalarov Development’s” second project in Uzbekistan and is aimed at boosting tourism and attracting residents, international visitors, and investors.

World.title: Kazakhstan eyes Finnish expertise to protect Caspian Sea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Kazakhstan is ready to consider a project developed by Finnish company Lamor Corporation to improve the environmental sustainability of the Caspian Sea, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources said.

The issue was discussed during a meeting in Astana between Kazakhstan's Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Yerlan Nyssanbayev and Finnish Parliament Member Ville Skinnari.

The Kazakh side expressed readiness to thoroughly review Lamor Corporation's concept once it is officially submitted.

" Kazakhstan supports the key areas of the project - environmental monitoring, oil spill response and ecosystem restoration - and welcomes an approach to its implementation under the leadership of Kazakhstan with the technical participation of Finnish partners," the ministry said.

The project is being discussed within the framework of Kazakhstan-Finland cooperation and environmental initiatives under the European Union's Global Gateway program.

The sides also discussed the possible participation of Finnish partners in other environmental projects in Kazakhstan, including the development of a regional forestry training center for Central Asian countries, Finnish water treatment technologies and cooperation between Kazhydromet and the Finnish Meteorological Institute.

The proposed forestry center, to be developed jointly with the UNDP near Astana, is expected to train more than 1,000 specialists annually, with its preliminary budget estimated at $40 million.

World.title: Man wielding sword injures several at school in Sweden
World.content:
A man armed with a sword has injured several people at a high school in central Sweden.

At least two people have sustained serious injuries, according to emergency services.

After 2.20pm, local time, reports came through of an attack at Brinellskolan school in the municipality of Fagersta.

The local government said a person entered the school with a sword and injured several people.

Police said they had one person in custody and were investigating the incident.

"A call was received regarding a case of ongoing deadly violence at a school in Fagersta," police said in a statement.

The high school has about 450 students aged between 16 and 20.

Fagersta has a population of about 13,000 people and is located roughly 170km north west of Stockholm.

The local government authority has opened a crisis centre, offering support and information.

The school had just opened after a summer break and for some students it marked the first day at the senior high school.

Several other schools and public buildings in Fagersta were also placed in lockdown after the alleged sword attack.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said police were working intensively on the case and asked everyone to let them and the emergency services work undisturbed.

"Our thoughts are with all those affected," he posted on social media.

The incident comes more than a year after a school shooting in Orebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself, in the worst mass shooting in Swedish history.

World.title: Prince Harry and others ordered to pay $17.8m legal costs to Daily Mail publisher
World.content:
Prince Harry, Elton John and a group of other high-profile claimants face the prospect of having to pay millions of pounds out of their own pockets to cover the legal costs of The Daily Mail's publisher, after a High Court judge ruled their failed privacy lawsuits were conducted in an unreasonable way.

The judge also ordered an interim payment of 9.54 million British pounds ($17.88 million) towards the legal costs of Associated Newspapers, which publishes The Daily Mail and other titles.

Last month, Justice Matthew Nicklin comprehensively rejected the case brought by Prince Harry, singer Elton John and five other figures, dismissing allegations that the Mail had engaged in widespread unlawful activities, such as phone hacking.

The Daily Mail's publisher argued Prince Harry and the other claimants had made wide-ranging, serious and "egregious" allegations against the paper without supporting evidence. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Friday's judgment delivered another damaging blow to the claimants, ruling that the outstanding amount should be paid on an "indemnity basis".

This means that, as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay an amount towards Associated's legal costs without the publisher needing to show these were reasonable and proportionate.

Explaining his decision, Justice Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants' case had been put, including that serious allegations had rested on "speculative and inferential" foundations.

"In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree," the judge said.

A spokesperson for Prince Harry did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters, while a spokesman for Associated Newspapers called the ruling "another overwhelming victory for the Mail and its journalism".

The court was told at a hearing in July that Associated had incurred a legal bill of 34.5 million British pounds ($65.6 million), while Prince Harry and other claimants only had an insurance policy which covered 16 million pounds ($30.4 million).

Associated's lawyer, Antony White, argued the claimants had made wide-ranging, serious and "egregious" allegations without supporting evidence, which had added to their costs.

He also said a statement made by the prince following the ruling was an abuse of his position and celebrity status.

Nicholas Bacon, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated's 34.5 million-pound legal bill was "eye-watering", far exceeding an agreed budget.

Reuters

World.title: Federal government to fund majority of ACT gun buyback scheme
World.content:
The ACT will introduce a gun buyback scheme similar to the one in NSW, as part of a national push to strengthen Australia's gun laws.

What we do and don't know about guns in Australia Gun control researchers say we have "no idea" how many black market and 3D-printed weapons are out there.

The agreement between the federal and ACT governments comes after a National Cabinet commitment to "eradicate" antisemitism and strengthen gun laws following the Bondi Beach terrorist attack in December last year.

Last week, NSW announced it would be the first state to begin the national buyback scheme, commencing on November 2.

The ACT committed to being part of the scheme after it was announced in the wake of the attack, but until now has remained in negotiation with the federal government over how it would be funded.

The agreement will see the Commonwealth government fund 75 per cent of the buyback and associated administrative costs, and 100 per cent of the firearm destruction costs, with the ACT government funding the rest.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says national gun reform is important to ensure terrorist attacks like the one in Bondi cannot occur again. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the scheme was about taking action to keep communities safe.

"National gun reform is an important part of making sure an antisemitic terrorist attack like we saw at Bondi can't happen again," Mr Albanese said.

" I thank the ACT government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians. "

Currently there are about 23,000 firearms in the ACT, and over 7,000 people who hold a firearms licence.

About 14 per cent of those licence holders are expected to be affected by the proposed firearms cap.

No further details have been given about what date the scheme will begin in the territory, or what compensation will be offered per surrendered firearm.

'Some of the strongest firearms laws in the country'

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr acknowledged that the majority of firearms owners were responsible and law-abiding. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In a statement, ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the agreement with the federal government strengthened community safety, and supported effective firearm reforms across jurisdictions.

"Reducing the number of high-risk firearms in circulation is a sensible and practical measure to help keep Canberrans safer," he said.

"Working with the Commonwealth and NSW ensures a more coordinated approach to firearms safety.

" The ACT has some of the strongest firearms laws in the country and this agreement supports our ongoing efforts to further reduce the risk of firearms falling into the wrong hands. "

Mr Barr acknowledged that "the overwhelming majority" of licensed gun owners were responsible and law-abiding citizens.

Along with committing to the national buyback scheme, the ACT has also proposed a change to its gun laws. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The buyback scheme will provide compensation while helping deliver further community safety outcomes," Mr Barr said.

The agreement also comes after the ACT government proposed new gun laws for the territory in February, which would see licensed gun holders limited to owning five guns.

The Firearms (Public Safety) Amendment Bill 2026 includes exemptions on that cap, allowing up to 10 guns for occupational and sporting purposes.

It would also criminalise the possession of blueprints for 3D-printed guns, prohibit belt-fed firearms, and re-categorise firearm types.

The bill is still before the ACT Legislative Assembly, and is expected to be debated during the assembly's spring sittings.

World.title: Tony Burke breaks silence on ex-ASIO agent's Bondi royal commission testimony
World.content:
A former ASIO agent who wants to give evidence to the Bondi royal commission can do so in open hearings, the Home Affairs minister says, meaning he does not need a visa to travel to Australia.

It is the first time Tony Burke has publicly addressed the man's intent to testify after previously denying his Australian visa request.

The former agent, known as Marcus, wants to give evidence about what he knew of the Bondi gunmen in the years before last December's terror attack.

He spent years infiltrating Islamic extremist groups in western Sydney, working as a paid source for domestic spy agency ASIO before his cover was blown.

Marcus met the Akrams when he infiltrated Sydney's Islamic State network for ASIO. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Marcus has repeatedly made a case to give evidence from within Australia, due both to the sensitivity of his evidence and the legal protections he gains from being on Australian soil.

The royal commission has previously held classified hearings to ensure it can take evidence on sensitive intelligence information.

Mr Burke told reporters this morning he had been advised any evidence Marcus gives can be heard in public and heard remotely.

"Mike Burgess, the director-general of ASIO, has advised and made clear to the royal commission that any evidence that would come from this particular individual is declassified," he said.

Ex-spy denied visa ahead of Bondi RC The man who previously warned ASIO about the Bondi gunmen will not be able to give sensitive and classified evidence at the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

"He's happy for it to be given in a complete public forum. It could be given over the phone on (Microsoft) Teams. It could be given in any way that the individual wants."

The royal commission has previously reached out to Marcus, it stated it is "eager" to hear his evidence and work out the best means for that to take place.

He is currently living abroad and cannot reach an Australian embassy.

Separately, NSW Police has also reached out to the former agent seeking assistance with its own investigations into last December's shooting.

Marcus has expressed fears for his personal safety while living overseas. He has sought protection and resettlement in Australia in the past.

His first visa application was rejected on the grounds that immigration authorities did not believe he had a genuine intention to leave the country, and his second application remains pending.

Mr Burke said the applications have followed all the normal channels.

"The department has its normal processes in working out whether or not someone qualifies for a visa under the Migration Act, and there hasn't been interference with that process," he said.

"The department looks at the Migration Act, looks at the application, and makes their own decision."

Advocates maintain call for visa

Whistleblower advocates have continued to back Marcus' cause, arguing the safest place for the former agent to give evidence is on Australian soil.

Marcus has previously told the ABC's Four Corners about his interactions with the Bondi gunmen, Sajid and Naveed Akram.

He claims he warned ASIO about the Akrams years before the attack.

ASIO has described the former agent as disgruntled and unreliable, but Marcus has rejected the characterisations.

Gabriel Shipton, from the whistleblower advocacy group the Information Rights Project, said he is in danger abroad.

Tense exchange at royal commission The witness, a Sydney researcher, questioned Israel's right to exist and was quizzed on her views comparing zionism to violent extremism.

"The protections offered by the royal commission do not extend outside Australia," he said.

"Marcus continues to risk his safety and the safety of his family. He is willing to give evidence and again the government is not acknowledging the threats he is under from the associates of the Akrams."

The group has provided support to the former agent as he lives overseas.

Mr Shipton said he should be allowed to give his evidence within Australia.

"The government has left it up to Information Rights to keep one of its ex-employees safe after years of undercover service, and again the minister has shown they are not serious about hearing evidence that contradicts the facts given by the institution in his own ministry."

World.title: 'Bittersweet': Vulnerable moment becomes national prize-winning photo
World.content:
Melbourne artist Nathan Beard has won the $30,000 National Photographic Portrait Prize for a faceless and intimate portrait of his aunty recuperating after a major medical scare.

Beard captured the private moment while visiting the beloved matriarch, Mae Khong, in Thailand earlier this year.

"On this particular trip she had suffered a fall at home and I was the only one in the house with her," he said.

The winning photograph in the 2026 National Photographic Portrait Prize, titled Mae Khong, by Melbourne artist Nathan Beard. (Supplied: Nathan Beard)

" She insisted that evening, even after the shock of the event, to bathe herself, and to do so independently. "

The National Portrait Gallery's Director of Curatorial and Collection, Isobel Parker Philip, said the photograph conveyed fortitude and strength, coupled with fatigue and vulnerability.

"You can't see her face but that doesn't mean you don't have an emotional connection to her," she said.

"You might look at it and see one of your loved ones; you can read the many, many years of her life experiences in the frame."

Mae died in July, meaning she will never know of the prestigious accolade bestowed on her nephew.

"It is bittersweet being recognised for the award because it's sort of a final gift of hers to me," Beard said.

NghỉNghiêm (AttentionAt ease), 2025 by Phuong Nguyen Le, winner of the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award. (Supplied: Phuong Nguyen Le)

The multidisciplinary artist, who draws on his Australian-Thai heritage, said his aunty was an influential figure in fostering his sense of cultural pride and belonging.

"She always struggled with why I would find her such a captivating subject," Beard said.

" She always thought it was silly that someone would think her worthy of that sort of status. "

Alongside the $30,000 prize money, Beard will also receive $20,000 worth of camera equipment.

UNTITLED_ 01 (Series_ What Remains_), by Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud, depicts a Flemington public housing resident packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition. (Supplied: Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud)

Moments of joy, humour, tenderness

The image is among 30 finalists selected in this year's National Photographic Portrait Prize from more than 1,000 entries.

The selection showcases a diverse array of styles and subjects, from moments of joy and humour to poignant and tender snapshots.

Sublim8 by Camille Perry, a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Camille Perry)

"It truly is a celebration of portraiture in its most expanded form," Ms Parker Philip said.

Phuong Nguyen Le won the $3,000 First Time Finalist Award for a portrait of his father, taken to mark the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War.

Earlier this week, Melbourne photographer Hussein Abdirahman Mohamud won the $3,000 Art Handlers' Award for his image of a Flemington public housing resident, packing to leave her home after it was earmarked for demolition.

Holding Space by Adam Edwards was a finalist in the National Photographic Portrait Prize 2026. (Supplied: Adam Edwards)

This National Photographic Portrait Prize was launched in 2007 and is open to emerging and established artists.

This year marks the final iteration of the competition in its current format, with a new prize model to be announced by the National Portrait Gallery in 2027.

Hanging alongside the 2026 show is a retrospective exhibition of almost two decades of finalists' work.

A portrait of actor David Howell by Ingvar Kenne was also a finalist. (Supplied: Ingvar Kenne)

It includes some famous faces, such as former prime minister Bob Hawke sipping a milkshake.

"Photography makes up about 57 per cent of our collection," Ms Parker Philip said.

"It's really important to the gallery and we're excited to support more photographers in the future."

World.title: McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies
World.content:
Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

The Lions went into the final round with a 2.2 per cent advantage over the Hawks.

A dominant display against the Magpies at the MCG saw the Lions emerge with a 63-point victory, 25.9 (159) to 15.6 (96) that gives them a 4.4 per cent lead over their rivals.

However Hawthorn has the advantage of playing West Coast in Perth on Sunday, needing a winning margin of somewhere in the region of 100 points to overtake the Lions.

Logan Morris kicked eight goals, and Irishman Conor McKenna kicked four, including a soccered dink of a goal in the first half, and a blind snap on the turn from 45 in the third quarter.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan told Fox Footy his side would "absolutely have taken it" if offered top-four at the start of the year.

Logan Morris is leading the way in attack for the Brisbane Lions against Collingwood at the MCG. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

Collingwood coach Craig McRae said the game was a hard watch at times as a coach given the lack of defence - the Pies kicked seven goals in a wide-open final term and the Lions booted nine.

But McRae was clear on what he and his team had seen from the Lions.

"Clearly we played the best team in the competition," he told reporters.

"They've got gears ... like we haven't seen a team do (this year), they can put you away so quickly."

Magpies great Scott Pendlebury is under an injury cloud after ending his game with a knee bursa issue.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Man accused of defrauding Indigenous community not of 'dishonest mind'
World.content:
Lawyers representing a man accused of defrauding money meant for an Indigenous community say his actions do not show a "dishonest mind" but a "best effort" to account for where the money went.

Ankumuthi traditional owner Larry Joe Woosup has been charged with two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. He has pleaded not guilty.

During the trial this week, the District Court in Cairns heard Mr Woosup and another community member arranged a deal with a mining company over the right to mine bauxite on traditional lands a year after a separate deal with the community reached a stalemate.

Mr Woosup then set up trust accounts with two different banks for the Ankumuthi community, where he was the sole trustee.

The jury was told it was an undisputed fact that Mr Woosup then used the overdraft capacity on one account to transfer and withdraw $110,000 and deposited a cheque for $95,000 from the mining company into the other account, which was then also withdrawn.

The requirement for both trusts was for all money to be used for the benefit of the Ankumuthi community, the court was told.

The crown case

Crown prosecutor Christian Peters told the jury Mr Woosup's dishonesty had been set out in "black and white".

Christian Peters (right) has told the court of Mr Woosup's multiple cash withdrawals. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

He said Mr Woosup was well and truly aware of his role as trustee and had been receiving advice every step of the way.

Mr Peters highlighted the various cash withdrawals from the multiple trust accounts, as well as some of the records of expenditure, including the purchase of three cars and numerous accommodation expenses.

Mr Peters also questioned the responses Mr Woosup gave in a questionnaire for federal court proceedings, where he listed a total of $13,000 in a fortnight as "personal expenses" and multiple cash withdrawals, each up to $5,000 in value, as non-specific "Trust bills".

"What bills? What bills was the trust paying?" Mr Peters said.

He also referenced some of Mr Woosup's conduct in the years after the alleged fraud, where other members of the Ankumuthi community confronted him about rumours he had taken money meant for the community.

The trial is expected to conclude with Judge Joshua Treviño KC's final closing statement on Monday. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

In one witness's recollection, Mr Woosup apologised and asked for forgiveness.

"That is an admission by him … that that money was not used for the principal purposes of that trust," Mr Peters said.

Mr Woosup's defence

Mr Woosup's defence barrister, Matt Jackson, told the court that when questions first started to be raised about where trust money was spent, Mr Woosup engaged an accountant and provided bank statements and receipts.

Mr Jackson suggested to the jury that this was a "pretty good effort" to engage with the process and indicated an "honest state of mind".

He said the prosecution had an issue with Mr Woosup's use of cash and said while Mr Peters had asserted the purpose would be to defy tracing, Mr Jackson insisted it was not uncommon for Mr Woosup to pay bills in cash.

Mr Jackson also questioned if the prosecution had truly provided any evidence the money had not gone back to the community.

He said the cars purchased had been used for cultural surveys on country, and that many of the witnesses called who said they had not received any money only became recognised as Native Title holders years after the events.

Larry Joe Woosup has pleaded not guilty to two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each. (ABC Far North: Holly Richardson)

The jury heard from Mr Jackson that the many errors in Mr Woosup's documentation were evidence of the passage of time, rather than dishonesty.

"This case is not about what the trust means … it's about what Larry Woosup meant," Mr Jackson said.

He said his conduct, including his denials and apologies to members of the Ankumuthi community after the events, was also consistent with the state of mind that he did not do anything wrong.

"People can apologise for a number of different reasons … it doesn't mean they're trying to hide," Mr Jackson said.

Judge Joshua Treviño KC has begun his summing up to the jury and will continue when court resumes on Monday.

World.title: Jury discharged in rape trial of competitive bull rider
World.content:
The jury in the rape trial of competitive bull rider Clay Benjamin Hall has been discharged after failing to reach a verdict on one of two charges in relation to an incident in Warwick in 2021.

After more than eight hours of deliberations the jury unanimously found Mr Hall not guilty of one count of rape but was unable to reach a verdict on a second count related to the same incident.

Justice Philip McCarthy KC discharged the jury today after it failed to reach a unanimous or majority verdict on the remaining charge.

The court was told Mr Hall met the girl, who was in her late teens at the time, on a street in Warwick, about 160 kilometres south-west of Brisbane, in the early hours of October 2021.

Prosecutors alleged Mr Hall, now 26, raped the teenager after she offered to show him a shortcut to the Warwick Showgrounds.

The court heard the teenager had been drinking and had been at a house party with people she did not know before she met Mr Hall.

Clay Benjamin Hall told police in 2023 that he had been given consent by the complainant. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Mr Hall was in Warwick to watch his brother compete at the Warwick Rodeo.

The court heard Mr Hall, who was not competing because of an injury, had also been drinking before walking to a service station to buy food in the early hours of the morning.

A key issue at trial was whether the sexual activity between Mr Hall and the complainant was consensual.

Defence barrister David Jones KC told the jury it was not in dispute that Mr Hall and the complainant had vaginal intercourse but rejected the allegation that anal penetration had occurred.

Jurors were shown a recording of a 2023 police interview in which Mr Hall said he propositioned the teenager and initially received no response but later he claimed was given consent.

The jury was also shown police interviews conducted with the complainant at hospital on the morning of the incident and later that day at a police station.

The complainant gave evidence during the trial and was cross-examined by the defence.

During deliberations jurors asked to view the complainant's recorded interviews again.

After more than eight hours of deliberations, Justice McCarthy gave the jury a majority verdict direction, allowing it to return a verdict if 11 jurors agreed and one disagreed.

But the jury later indicated it was unable to reach a majority verdict.

While discharging the jury, Justice McCarthy thanked jurors for their work.

"Whilst you may have a frustration, you worked very hard. Your endeavour was appreciated and I appreciated the way you took upon your task in this courtroom," he said.

The unresolved charge remains before the court and the matter will return to the Warwick District Court for a callover on September 17.

World.title: Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry, celebrities ordered to pay $18m – but final court bill could be higher David Crowe August 22, 2026 — 1:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prince Harry has been ordered to pay a steep legal bill for his failed court case against a major publisher after a court ruled that he and his fellow claimants owed £9.54 million ($18.1 million) in legal costs. The court ruling exposes Harry and others, including rock star Elton John and model Elizabeth Hurley, to even greater costs after a judge dismissed their long-running claim against the Daily Mail earlier this year. Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, at a roundtable for support for veterans in Washington on Wednesday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon They must pay the first sum by August 28 and face a difficult legal argument over the remainder of the costs, given the Mail’s publisher won the case and wants the prince and others to cover its costs. Lawyers for the publisher, Associated Newspapers, told the court in July that its legal bill had reached £34.5 million ($65.6 million).



Related Article Royal family ‘Obvious whitewash’: Prince Harry lashes judge after losing Daily Mail privacy case Harry and other claimants arranged an insurance policy to cover £16 ⁠million ($30 million), but are now exposed to a much steeper bill that could require them to pay from their own savings. Judge Matthew Nicklin’s judgment on costs was published on Friday in London (early on Saturday AEST). Nicklin was highly critical of the way the claimants’ case had been put, saying their allegations were based on “speculative and inferential” foundations and had not been withdrawn when they were no longer being pursued. “In my judgment, the cumulative effect of these matters takes the case well outside the norm. The conduct was unreasonable to a high degree,” Nicklin said.



The High Court ruled in July that the Duke of Sussex and the other claimants had failed to prove their allegations that the Daily Mail had used unlawful means, including phone hacking, to get stories about them. They also claimed it used “blagging” – a practice in which a journalist makes false claims to trick people into divulging information. Associated Newspapers said at the time that the ruling was “an overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists and for a free press generally”. The claimants who joined Harry in the case were Hurley, actor Sadie Frost, politician Simon Hughes and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, a member of the House of Lords whose son was murdered in a racist attack. John joined the case with his husband, David Furnish. Actor and model Elizabeth Hurley arrives at court with her son, Damian, in January. AFP



All of them claimed Associated Newspapers had used illegal means to gain information about them.

The judge found that the claims by the prince and others relied on “inference” rather than hard evidence. Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious “But suspicion, even where understandable, was not enough,” he wrote. Harry issued an angry statement after the July decision, with his fellow claimant Baroness Lawrence. “It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted,” they said.



“When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing, despite the documents showing otherwise, then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.” Lawyers for the newspaper called that statement as an abuse of the prince’s celebrity status. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? The newspaper is controlled by Jonathan Vere Harmsworth, the hereditary peer Viscount Rothermere, whose great-grandfather founded the Daily Mail in 1896. In a statement on Friday, the publisher hailed the initial decision on costs as another “overwhelming victory” for the Mail and its journalism.



If the two sides cannot agree on the rest of the costs, they will head to separate litigation to decide the bill. Nicholas Bacon, KC, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated’s £34.5 million ($65.6 million) legal bill was “eye-watering” and ⁠far exceeding an agreed budget. World.title: The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers Michael Gleeson August 22, 2026 — 1:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Scott Pendlebury jogged slowly to the bench favouring his leg. It might be the last time he is seen in a Collingwood jumper on the MCG. It was an utterly nondescript moment in the most storied of careers. Pendlebury felt a strain at the back of his knee that might have been a bursar, might have been a hamstring strain, and might just be the injury that puts a stop on his finals series. Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. Getty Images Last year’s preliminary final has to be in Craig McRae’s mind as he ponders the fitness of probably the club’s greatest-ever player. Last year, also against the Brisbane Lions, he tore a calf in the warm-up. A soft tissue injury again for a now 38-year-old, on the eve of the finals, will weigh on McRae. And Pendlebury. If it is to be his last game for Collingwood, it could not have been a more anticlimactic departure. No garlands, no lines of honour, no chairing off, no kids through the banner, just a night sitting on the bench in his slides, eating chicken wraps and watching his team get belted.



It was the sort of moment that might encourage the idea that we don’t want him to go out this way – and he doesn’t either – so he plays on. As McRae said, those are conversations for another day. But that moment punctuated what was a very strange game. View post on X The AFL expanded the finals to 10 teams and introduced the wildcard round to engender interest in the last rounds of the home-and-away season. Ironically, this game would have had more interest were it held under last year’s rules. Collingwood could not drop below 10th, and so were battling to finish either eighth or ninth. In other words, last year they would have had to win to play finals. Instead, this game was played with the passion of a polka.



Collingwood’s game is predicated on furious intensity and defensive fight. None were present in a game where 40 goals were kicked and no one wanted to defend. It was a case for the prosecution who say high scoring and exciting football are two different things. View post on X That is not to diminish the Lions’ effort for they outplayed Collingwood. They beat them by 54 points earlier this year and they are plainly a better team. But we knew that. One team has won the past two flags and sits now in third place, and Collingwood needed a wildcard round to be sure of playing finals. “It was really hard as a coach because you’re seeing us not do things we’ve been doing,” McRae said. “I go, ‘Oh, what are we doing? Like, this is a trademark’ … I think there was a period of the game where it looked like both teams wanted to get to next week quickly. It can happen this time of year for teams that aren’t playing for much.”



Logan Morris is still only scratching the surface of what he could become. AFL Photos As it was, the interest was in Logan Morris. It is exciting – or frightening, depending on your perspective – to think that Morris has two flags already and is yet to even get close to being the dominant player he is becoming. There was a world in which Morris might have been at Collingwood. If the idea of what the club missed out on has haunted them since, the reality of what he has become was a living nightmare on the MCG. Morris kicked eight and could have had 10. In his draft year – and yes, every other club with a selection would have taken him before pick No.31 had they known what he would become – Collingwood agonised over the decision but were troubled that he was an in-between size and would not be a key forward. They chose Harry De Mattia instead at No.25. He is yet to play a senior game. Morris was outstanding, and with Oscar Allen and Eric Hipwood they had their way with Collingwood’s depleted backline missing Darcy Moore, Isaac Quaynor and Harry Perryman and with Jeremy Howe on managed minutes.



Liam Puncher was playing SANFL footy only a couple of months ago. He might have preferred West Torrens after the night he had on the MCG with the ball coming in the way it was. Lachie Neale played the sort of game that would have had the boxes of both coaches asking questions. Chris Fagan will have looked at his 16 clearances, yes 16, and wondered, ‘How can we let him and Zac Bailey potentially leave?’ Craig Mcrae and Collingwood will have said, ‘If we had misgivings about a 32-year-old free agent before, we don’t now’. For the Lions, this game was about jockeying to try and make sure they played the team everyone now wants to play in the finals, Sydney. They should have safeguarded that. The draw with Collingwood last week is all the more galling for the Hawks this week, given the Swans are now a shattered club and a team you’d far rather play than any other in these finals (this is obviously an observation through a football lens on the season, and plainly not a comment on what occurred in the Pullman hotel to precipitate this change at Sydney).



Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘We were keen on him, the coaches weren’t’: How this star slipped to the Lions The Hawks now need to win by nigh on 100 points over West Coast to boost their percentage enough to jump the Lions and play Sydney in the first final, not Fremantle in WA. Its doable, but the way they played last week you would not think likely unless the Eagles play like they want their holidays to start. That is the hard bit for interpreting this game. The Lions showed they are exceptional and have as complete a forward set-up, with the best young key forward in the game, as they do defensive set-up. They don’t lack for anything across the ground, other than perhaps some smarts from Ty Gallop, a player just back from an idiotic three-game suspension for slamming Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf, only to tackle Charlie West into the ground with both arms pinned. But then Dayne Zorko elbowing Jack Crisp in the face with a late smother of a handball is also a contender for unnecessarily risky actions. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury
World.content:
World No.1 Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open due to a persistent right knee injury, the Italian said on Friday, depriving the season’s final grand slam of one of its biggest contenders.

The 24-year-old, who captured his fifth major title at Wimbledon last month, has not played since sustaining the injury earlier this month.

Jannik Sinner successfully defended his Wimbledon title in July. Getty

He pulled out of the Cincinnati Open and also skipped the Canadian Open, two key hard-court tune-up events ahead of the grand slam tournament in New York.

“Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner said in a statement on X.

World.title: The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated
World.content:
PoliticsNSWMedia & marketing The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated August 21, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. The awards, across 37 total categories, were announced at a ceremony at Sydney’s Royal Randwick Racecourse on Friday night. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Edwina Pickles Senior sports reporter Chris Barrett won the Outstanding Sport Reporting category for an investigation revealing rugby league’s most high-profile referee, Ashley Klein, had a $400,000 gambling problem, which the code knew about for four years while letting him continue to officiate matches at the top level. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Among his submissions was “The lying, the Ferrari wish and $400,000 in cash in the wardrobe”, which related to chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont’s coverage of former bankrupt Warren Jack’s “fanciful” explanations to a Sydney court during a dispute over unpaid loans. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. The Age’s veteran crime reporter, John Silvester, also won Outstanding Columnist for his regular Naked City column lifting the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld.



The Herald was nominated for a total of 20 awards, the most of any news organisation in Australia, winning five categories. Related Article Media & marketing Herald scoops young journalist prizes Herald editor Jordan Baker said she was enormously proud of the publication’s winners and finalists. “The recognition of the Herald across so many areas – sport reporting, feature writing, headlines, photography and cartoons – illustrates the depth of talent in our newsroom. “It is also a reflection of the Herald’s commitment to serving our subscribers and telling Sydney’s stories,” Baker said.



The foundation said the 2026 awards attracted a record number of entries. “It’s been another bumper year for excellent Australian journalism, and there’s no greater honour than to receive a Kennedy for your work,” Kennedy Foundation chair Carl Dumbrell said. “The Kennedy Foundation is extremely proud of its support for those endeavours that are essential to an informed and vital democracy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOrganised crime Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week James Costa August 21, 2026 — 10:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been injured in a drive-by shooting outside a cafe in Melbourne’s west. Victoria Police are investigating Friday night’s non-fatal shooting that happened at about 7.15pm on Borrack Square in Altona North. The victim, who is yet to be identified, was taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. No arrests have been made and police were told the offender or offenders fled the scene in a vehicle. It is the third shooting in Borrack Square this year.



Last week, gangland boss Fadi Haddara was ambushed and shot in the face, stomach and chest outside his Altona North home. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Haddara, 48, was found lying in a pool of blood by a family member next to a parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, before 8pm on Sunday. Police said the attack was targeted and are on alert for retaliatory attacks, but are keeping an open mind about the shooting’s connection to Melbourne’s tobacco war. In May, shots were fired into a tobacco store at Borrack square just after 5.30pm.



A 49-year-old man was shot in the arm and taken to a hospital, which police suspected was linked to the Melbourne’s illicit tobacco war. In March, the same square was shot up in a brazen late-night shooting, believed to be linked to the city’s ongoing tobacco war. CCTV footage showed a group of panicked men toppling a table and chairs and running inside to escape the bullets. One man climbed through the cafe’s window, while another two took shelter in corners outside the business. When police arrived, they said they found a 49-year-old man who had been shot twice in the arm. He was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. They also claimed it used “blagging” – a practice in which a journalist makes false claims to trick people into divulging information. Associated Newspapers said at the time that the ruling was “an overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists and for a free press generally”. The claimants who joined Harry in the case were Hurley, actor Sadie Frost, politician Simon Hughes and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, a member of the House of Lords whose son was murdered in a racist attack. John joined the case with his husband, David Furnish. Actor and model Elizabeth Hurley arrives at court with her son, Damian, in January. AFP



All of them claimed Associated Newspapers had used illegal means to gain information about them.

The judge found that the claims by the prince and others relied on “inference” rather than hard evidence. Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious “But suspicion, even where understandable, was not enough,” he wrote. Harry issued an angry statement after the July decision, with his fellow claimant Baroness Lawrence. “It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted,” they said.



“When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing, despite the documents showing otherwise, then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.” Lawyers for the newspaper called that statement as an abuse of the prince’s celebrity status. Related Article Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? The newspaper is controlled by Jonathan Vere Harmsworth, the hereditary peer Viscount Rothermere, whose great-grandfather founded the Daily Mail in 1896. In a statement on Friday, the publisher hailed the initial decision on costs as another “overwhelming victory” for the Mail and its journalism.



If the two sides cannot agree on the rest of the costs, they will head to separate litigation to decide the bill. Nicholas Bacon, KC, the lawyer for the claimants, said in their submissions that Associated’s £34.5 million ($65.6 million) legal bill was “eye-watering” and ⁠far exceeding an agreed budget. With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 The moment that might have ended the most storied of Collingwood careers Michael Gleeson August 22, 2026 — 1:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Scott Pendlebury jogged slowly to the bench favouring his leg. It might be the last time he is seen in a Collingwood jumper on the MCG. It was an utterly nondescript moment in the most storied of careers. Pendlebury felt a strain at the back of his knee that might have been a bursar, might have been a hamstring strain, and might just be the injury that puts a stop on his finals series. Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. Getty Images Last year’s preliminary final has to be in Craig McRae’s mind as he ponders the fitness of probably the club’s greatest-ever player. Last year, also against the Brisbane Lions, he tore a calf in the warm-up. A soft tissue injury again for a now 38-year-old, on the eve of the finals, will weigh on McRae. And Pendlebury. If it is to be his last game for Collingwood, it could not have been a more anticlimactic departure. No garlands, no lines of honour, no chairing off, no kids through the banner, just a night sitting on the bench in his slides, eating chicken wraps and watching his team get belted.



It was the sort of moment that might encourage the idea that we don’t want him to go out this way – and he doesn’t either – so he plays on. As McRae said, those are conversations for another day. But that moment punctuated what was a very strange game. View post on X The AFL expanded the finals to 10 teams and introduced the wildcard round to engender interest in the last rounds of the home-and-away season. Ironically, this game would have had more interest were it held under last year’s rules. Collingwood could not drop below 10th, and so were battling to finish either eighth or ninth. In other words, last year they would have had to win to play finals. Instead, this game was played with the passion of a polka.



Collingwood’s game is predicated on furious intensity and defensive fight. None were present in a game where 40 goals were kicked and no one wanted to defend. It was a case for the prosecution who say high scoring and exciting football are two different things. View post on X That is not to diminish the Lions’ effort for they outplayed Collingwood. They beat them by 54 points earlier this year and they are plainly a better team. But we knew that. One team has won the past two flags and sits now in third place, and Collingwood needed a wildcard round to be sure of playing finals. “It was really hard as a coach because you’re seeing us not do things we’ve been doing,” McRae said. “I go, ‘Oh, what are we doing? Like, this is a trademark’ … I think there was a period of the game where it looked like both teams wanted to get to next week quickly. It can happen this time of year for teams that aren’t playing for much.”



Logan Morris is still only scratching the surface of what he could become. AFL Photos As it was, the interest was in Logan Morris. It is exciting – or frightening, depending on your perspective – to think that Morris has two flags already and is yet to even get close to being the dominant player he is becoming. There was a world in which Morris might have been at Collingwood. If the idea of what the club missed out on has haunted them since, the reality of what he has become was a living nightmare on the MCG. Morris kicked eight and could have had 10. In his draft year – and yes, every other club with a selection would have taken him before pick No.31 had they known what he would become – Collingwood agonised over the decision but were troubled that he was an in-between size and would not be a key forward. They chose Harry De Mattia instead at No.25. He is yet to play a senior game. Morris was outstanding, and with Oscar Allen and Eric Hipwood they had their way with Collingwood’s depleted backline missing Darcy Moore, Isaac Quaynor and Harry Perryman and with Jeremy Howe on managed minutes.



Liam Puncher was playing SANFL footy only a couple of months ago. He might have preferred West Torrens after the night he had on the MCG with the ball coming in the way it was. Lachie Neale played the sort of game that would have had the boxes of both coaches asking questions. Chris Fagan will have looked at his 16 clearances, yes 16, and wondered, ‘How can we let him and Zac Bailey potentially leave?’ Craig Mcrae and Collingwood will have said, ‘If we had misgivings about a 32-year-old free agent before, we don’t now’. For the Lions, this game was about jockeying to try and make sure they played the team everyone now wants to play in the finals, Sydney. They should have safeguarded that. The draw with Collingwood last week is all the more galling for the Hawks this week, given the Swans are now a shattered club and a team you’d far rather play than any other in these finals (this is obviously an observation through a football lens on the season, and plainly not a comment on what occurred in the Pullman hotel to precipitate this change at Sydney).



Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘We were keen on him, the coaches weren’t’: How this star slipped to the Lions The Hawks now need to win by nigh on 100 points over West Coast to boost their percentage enough to jump the Lions and play Sydney in the first final, not Fremantle in WA. Its doable, but the way they played last week you would not think likely unless the Eagles play like they want their holidays to start. That is the hard bit for interpreting this game. The Lions showed they are exceptional and have as complete a forward set-up, with the best young key forward in the game, as they do defensive set-up. They don’t lack for anything across the ground, other than perhaps some smarts from Ty Gallop, a player just back from an idiotic three-game suspension for slamming Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf, only to tackle Charlie West into the ground with both arms pinned. But then Dayne Zorko elbowing Jack Crisp in the face with a late smother of a handball is also a contender for unnecessarily risky actions. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: World No.1 Jannik Sinner withdraws from US Open due to injury
World.content:
World No.1 Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open due to a persistent right knee injury, the Italian said on Friday, depriving the season’s final grand slam of one of its biggest contenders.

The 24-year-old, who captured his fifth major title at Wimbledon last month, has not played since sustaining the injury earlier this month.

Jannik Sinner successfully defended his Wimbledon title in July. Getty

He pulled out of the Cincinnati Open and also skipped the Canadian Open, two key hard-court tune-up events ahead of the grand slam tournament in New York.

“Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner said in a statement on X.

World.title: The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated
World.content:
PoliticsNSWMedia & marketing The Herald picks up five awards as excellence in journalism celebrated August 21, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An investigation that revealed the NRL’s top referee had a gambling problem, photographs capturing the Bondi Beach terror attack, and a profile of Australia’s cardboard king are part of the Herald’s award-winning coverage celebrated at the Kennedy Foundation’s Excellence in Journalism awards. The awards, across 37 total categories, were announced at a ceremony at Sydney’s Royal Randwick Racecourse on Friday night. Edwina Pickles has been recognised for her photographic coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack. Edwina Pickles Senior sports reporter Chris Barrett won the Outstanding Sport Reporting category for an investigation revealing rugby league’s most high-profile referee, Ashley Klein, had a $400,000 gambling problem, which the code knew about for four years while letting him continue to officiate matches at the top level. Photographer Edwina Pickles won the Outstanding News Photography category for her coverage of the Bondi Beach terror attack in December.



Deputy state topic editor Michael Ruffles won the Outstanding Three Headlines category. Among his submissions was “The lying, the Ferrari wish and $400,000 in cash in the wardrobe”, which related to chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont’s coverage of former bankrupt Warren Jack’s “fanciful” explanations to a Sydney court during a dispute over unpaid loans. Cartoonist Matt Golding picked up the Outstanding Cartoon award for “Playing Trump”, which depicted Russian President Vladimir Putin passing the dice to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the pair play a board game called “Trump” with North Korea’s Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Cartoonist Matt Golding has been won for his “Playing Trump” cartoon. Matt Golding Jane Cadzow won Outstanding Feature Writing for “In The Box Seat”, her Good Weekend profile of cardboard king Anthony Pratt, the boss of Visy packaging and one of Australia’s richest men, published in the Herald and The Age. The Age’s veteran crime reporter, John Silvester, also won Outstanding Columnist for his regular Naked City column lifting the lid on Australia’s criminal underworld.



The Herald was nominated for a total of 20 awards, the most of any news organisation in Australia, winning five categories. Related Article Media & marketing Herald scoops young journalist prizes Herald editor Jordan Baker said she was enormously proud of the publication’s winners and finalists. “The recognition of the Herald across so many areas – sport reporting, feature writing, headlines, photography and cartoons – illustrates the depth of talent in our newsroom. “It is also a reflection of the Herald’s commitment to serving our subscribers and telling Sydney’s stories,” Baker said.



The foundation said the 2026 awards attracted a record number of entries. “It’s been another bumper year for excellent Australian journalism, and there’s no greater honour than to receive a Kennedy for your work,” Kennedy Foundation chair Carl Dumbrell said. “The Kennedy Foundation is extremely proud of its support for those endeavours that are essential to an informed and vital democracy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOrganised crime Altona North rocked by second shooting in a week James Costa August 21, 2026 — 10:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been injured in a drive-by shooting outside a cafe in Melbourne’s west. Victoria Police are investigating Friday night’s non-fatal shooting that happened at about 7.15pm on Borrack Square in Altona North. The victim, who is yet to be identified, was taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. No arrests have been made and police were told the offender or offenders fled the scene in a vehicle. It is the third shooting in Borrack Square this year.



Last week, gangland boss Fadi Haddara was ambushed and shot in the face, stomach and chest outside his Altona North home. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Haddara, 48, was found lying in a pool of blood by a family member next to a parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, before 8pm on Sunday. Police said the attack was targeted and are on alert for retaliatory attacks, but are keeping an open mind about the shooting’s connection to Melbourne’s tobacco war. In May, shots were fired into a tobacco store at Borrack square just after 5.30pm.



A 49-year-old man was shot in the arm and taken to a hospital, which police suspected was linked to the Melbourne’s illicit tobacco war. In March, the same square was shot up in a brazen late-night shooting, believed to be linked to the city’s ongoing tobacco war. CCTV footage showed a group of panicked men toppling a table and chairs and running inside to escape the bullets. One man climbed through the cafe’s window, while another two took shelter in corners outside the business. When police arrived, they said they found a 49-year-old man who had been shot twice in the arm. He was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
