World.title: MBIE backs council ruling that Christchurch Airbnb owners need to get consent or stop
World.content:
The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) has ruled that Christchurch unit owners have to ask for permission to offer the property as an Airbnb - or stop.

Christchurch City Council sought a determination from the ministry because it felt the owners, named in the determination as T Denman and K Suter, had changed the use of the unit from its consented use as a household unit, by making it available for short-term accommodation.

The unit, on Gloucester St, was issued a code compliance certificate in May 2025 as a multi-unit dwelling.

It is on the ground floor with a separate unit above.

The council told MBIE that it did not have evidence the unit had ever been used for its consented use and had been advertised online as visitor accommodation. The unit could be booked for one group at a time and one night or more.

The council contacted the owners in March telling them that the unit had changed from a residential classification to accommodation.

They had breached two requirements of the Building Act, in that they should have given notice of change of use, and that they could not change the use of the building unless the council gave them written notice that the new use would comply with the relevant provisions of the building code.

It issued a notice to fix, which said the owners should notify the council of the change, supply required documentation, and receive written notice that the new use would comply with the rules as required.

Alternatively, they would have to stop using the building for accommodation and return it to its residential use.

The owners said they had sought advice from the council before they started letting the unit and were told it would not be considered a change of use.

They had told the council they wanted to make it a short-term rental so they could use it as a holiday home.

MBIE principal adviser determinations Rebecca Mackie said there was no dispute the council had not approved a change.

There was also no dispute that the multi-unit residential building was consented as sleeping residential.

The question was whether the use had changed.

Mackie found that it had, because the unit was advertised at a nightly rate.

"In this case, the unit is not occupied as the exclusive home or residence of a household... The unit is made available to members of the public as short-term accommodation through an online accommodation platform, with different occupants able to stay on a nightly or weekly basis. That pattern of occupation is transient, rotational and commercial in character. Although each booking may involve only one person or one group staying at a time, there is no continuity of occupation by any particular household.

"The purpose of the use is to rent the unit out as temporary accommodation. That use is materially different from the purpose of the Housing category.... nor do I consider the low level of services provided is determinative of the use of the unit."

Mackie said the unit's use group had changed and there were additional or more onerous building code requirements with the new rules.

"The owners did not provide written notice to the authority under section 114, and the use was changed without written notice from the authority under section 115 that the building in its new use complies to the extent required, in contravention of these sections of the Act. Therefore, there was a basis to issue the notice to fix under section 164."

She upheld the council's notice to fix.

Consultant Mike Blackburn said the determination was relevant to apartments in other developments that were used predominantly as short-term accommodation.

"Where Council determines that a change of use has occurred, the Building Act process can also bring additional Building Code requirements into consideration. In this case MBIE specifically identified requirements relating to access and facilities for people with disabilities as an example of requirements applying to the new use. For developers, designers, property owners and operators involved in this part of the market, Determination 2026/026 is therefore one worth being aware of."

World.title: Hamilton man Jason Monkley charged childcare firm $2900 to fix van - then torched it
World.content:
A man who was trusted to repair a childcare van instead drove it to Hamilton Gardens and set it alight, only to be caught by his own CCTV footage.

Jason Paul Monkley had spent months fixing the Ōtorohanga-based Kiwi Kids Club van.

The owner had shelled out $2900 for materials, but after telling her the work was done and he would take it for a warrant, Monkley instead drove the van to Hamilton Gardens in the dead of night and torched it.

His actions led to a charge of arson, and this week Monkley appeared in Hamilton District Court for sentencing before Judge Stephen Clark.

Court documents state Monkley twice denied any involvement in the blaze. However, his movements were tracked to the minute by the city council, BP and his own CCTV system.

The court heard the victim had arranged for Monkley to fix her company van in mid to late 2024. Over the following months, she paid $2900 for the work to be completed.

By 13 May, 2025, the van was ready to be picked up. Monkley contacted the victim and said he needed to take it for a warrant of fitness.

However, at 3.02am on 15 May, Monkley was spotted on his CCTV system leaving his house with a red petrol container in his Ford.

He was caught on CCTV at BP Whitiora 20 minutes later, before he returned home.

At 4.46am, he was seen putting a bike and a clear plastic container into the back of the van before driving off.

He drove through Gate 1 at Hamilton Gardens at 5.32am and parked the van near the main car park. He set it on fire soon after and then rode his bike home.

Police received a call about the fire at 5.51am from a member of the public.

When spoken to, Monkley denied any involvement and said the van was stolen from outside his house.

He was questioned a second time and told officers he had left it outside an associate's property, from where it was stolen.

Monkley, a sickness beneficiary, had earlier accepted a sentence indication, and his counsel Glen Prentice said nothing in a pre-sentence report suggested he was unsuitable for home detention. He had been on bail with no issues, and he could immediately pay the reparation of $3400, which included a $500 insurance excess.

Judge Clark read excerpts from the victim impact statement in which she said she had trusted Monkley.

She ran the childcare programme in Te Kūiti and Ōtorohanga "with little to no support from the community" and was "flabbergasted" by his actions.

While Monkley's motive was not discussed in court, the victim said he could have told her he was "having issues".

"She says she was somewhat stunned and disappointed, and you could have worked it out as she described you as a family friend."

Judge Clark said he could not see anything in his pre-sentence report that would warrant further credit, except perhaps the fact Monkley had offered to pay the reparation in full.

For that, and his plea, the judge sentenced Monkley to nine months' home detention from a starting point of 19 months' jail.

The judge ordered the reparation be paid within 14 days.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: East Coast conservationist rescues emu chicks after feral cat attack
World.content:
An East Coast conservationist has become a surrogate dad to a couple of emu chicks, rescuing them after a feral cat attacked their nest.

Ruatoria man Graeme Atkins took the chicks in after inadvertently scaring away their real father.

"I was down the beach collecting firewood for a birthday celebration and scared the dad off the nest," he told Checkpoint.

"It was a bit of a bummer that that happened," he said, explaining that male emus look after the eggs and raise the chicks.

After a restless night spent worrying about the birds, he returned to the nest and saw a feral cat had attacked.

"Out of the five chicks I saw the day before only two were left," he said.

So he took action, taking them in despite "a little bit of trepidation about what we were getting into".

The chicks have made themselves at home on Atkins' property. Supplied

Raising them was similar to raising puppies, he said, as the chicks squeaked beside him.

"We've got so much advice from people who know emus.

"They're pretty endearing as a pet, they grow on you," he said.

The chicks are three weeks old now, and spend their days following Atkins around. He has created a warm home for them in a fenced-in enclosure outside his house.

"Because it's been so cold I put them inside a box that's got wool matting, and then some dry grass."

They have quickly made themselves at home - and developed a taste for some of the rare plants on Atkins' property.

"In six months they could be up to five feet tall," he said.

World.title: ACT to campaign on Paul Henry's 'Starship for cancer' proposal
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to build New Zealand's first dedicated national cancer centre, turning a musing from new candidate Paul Henry into a campaign promise.

ACT would establish a philanthropic foundation to attract some of the funding, and get rid of a cap on donation tax credits - the same cap that put one National MP at odds with his party.

When he announced his candidacy in July, Henry said he wanted a world-class cancer hospital in New Zealand, but admitted it would cost "multiple billions" of dollars.

"I think you could easily get a group of wealthy New Zealanders to stump up with about 10 billion, easily. The rest of it we would borrow, but that would be an investment in New Zealand's future," he said at the time.

Now, the party has confirmed it is pressing ahead with the idea, unveiling a plan to build a "Starship for Cancer" with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.

"Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer," Henry said.

Henry said Starship Children's Hospital in Auckland showed what the country could achieve when it concentrated on a single mission. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

The former broadcaster confessed he had announced the policy "on the fly" last month, and had expected to be pulled aside and discouraged.

"Instead I was told, 'we think you might be onto something'," he told an audience in Christchurch.

ACT expected around $2 billion of capital investment would be required.

"When I mentioned this out of the blue standing next to David Seymour at the press conference, I suggested we might be looking at a figure close to $10 billion, so ACT's involvement has already saved the country $8 billion," Henry said.

ACT would legislate to establish a not-for-profit, independent National Cancer Centre Foundation with charitable status.

To attract donations, ACT would remove the cap on donation tax credits.

The cap was criticised by National MP Greg Fleming on Thursday, who said work was underway to "fix" it, but revenue minister Simon Watts has insisted there are no plans to change it.

A policy document explained the centres would be funded through a combination of public-private partnership financing, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment, and other private capital "where appropriate".

The Department of Cancer Sciences at the University of Auckland and the Christchurch Cancer Foundation would work on business cases for the campuses.

Henry admitted he announced the policy "on the fly". RNZ

Health New Zealand would be a "major customer" of the centre, with ACT expecting it would relocate its existing cancer services in Auckland and Christchurch to the new campuses.

The Crown's ongoing financial liability would come through Health New Zealand purchasing the clinical services and using the facilities.

"This expenditure, to a significant extent, would otherwise need to occur elsewhere in the health system. In the future, medical

tourism from overseas could help subsidise the Centre's operations," the document said.

Henry said the campaign policy was "aspirational" but insisted it was realistic and practical.

"Comprehensive cancer centres are the gold standard internationally because they bring researchers, clinicians, universities, private providers and philanthropists together with world-class treatment, technology and clinical trials," he said.

World.title: Lawyer convicted of assault on his 12-year-old son which left him hospitalised
World.content:
A lawyer has been convicted and granted name suppression following a serious assault on his son that required him being hospitalised.

The lawyer, aged in his 50s, appeared in the Timaru District Court on Friday before Judge Campbell Savage where he was sentenced to supervision after pleading guilty to a charge of assault on a child.

The judge said the case, which began in 2022, had moved at "glacial pace".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Court documents obtained by RNZ detail the offending which occurred in April 2022.

The summary of facts said the lawyer and his son were boxing on a concrete area at the rear of their address.

The lawyer was a "fully grown man and the victim is a small built, 38kg 12-year-old child," the summary said.

Both were wearing boxing gloves.

The lawyer struck the victim's head causing him to bleed.

"The victim said 'please stop. I am serious'.

"The defendant then struck the victim in the face followed by the stomach. This caused the victim to cry. He went to the ground.

"The defendant continued to punch the victim on the ground. Eventually the victim said he could not breath and the defendant stopped. The victim then jumped the fence to get away."

The victim was taken to hospital and was initially diagnosed with a suspected fractured cheekbone and perforated liver, however after scans this was not the case.

He sustained extensive bruising to his head and ears and a cut above his eye.

He was admitted to hospital for three nights to allow observation and investigation of his possible injuries.

The lawyer declined to comment to police.

At sentencing the man's lawyer, Michael Sandom told the court the lawyer appeared before the court as a defendant and as a practicing lawyer.

The lawyer was convicted at Timaru District Court. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Sandom said he was appearing among many of his colleagues and peers, which brought a level of "embarrassment and shame".

"[He] is not a perfect person, but none of us are.

"He knows the mistake that he made, he is remorseful for what occurred and in my submission shame for what occurred is an important theme for this sentencing."

Sandom said the offending would stay with the lawyer "for the rest of his life".

The offending was "distressing and repugnant" to the lawyer.

"He's ashamed for what occurred. He can barely face it, can barely talk about it, can barely engage with it at all."

Sandom said the lawyer was a "kind and generous person" as well as an "advocate" in the criminal jurisdiction.

He accepted it was "serious" offending.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae said the Crown opposed the lawyer's application for a discharge without conviction and said his affidavit for name suppression did not meet the threshold.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. (File photo) Stuff / Pool / Alden Williams

Judge Savage said the matter had passed through the court system "at glacial pace", with the first hearing in April 2022.

The lawyer pleaded guilty during a trial after the victim had given evidence. Judge Savage said the lawyer's claim he did not see his son's statement until trial was "implausible".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Judge Savage said it was "charitable" to say the lawyer's guilty plea came at the 11th hour.

"It came as the clock was striking 12."

He said he had no doubt the lawyer loved his son "with all your heart".

In terms of aggravating factors, the judge pointed to the victim's age and the breach of trust.

Judge Savage declined to discharge the lawyer without a conviction, but did grant final name suppression.

He said he did not see the lawyer as a risk of re-offending.

The lawyer has been practicing for more than a decade. The New Zealand Law Society register does not say whether he holds a practicing certificate.

RNZ asked the New Zealand Law Society how the lawyer was able to continue practicing while the matter was before the court.

A spokesperson said the Law Society took any concerns regarding criminal offending by lawyers "seriously".

"Personal conduct by a lawyer may be considered under the complaints and disciplinary framework in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 (the Act) in certain circumstances.

"However, a lawyer who holds a current practising certificate and admits to, or is found guilty of, criminal offending is not automatically suspended from practice."

The spokesperson said concerns or complaints must first be considered by independent Standards Committees who may refer matters to the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal, if the conduct was "sufficiently serious".

"In addition, section 40 of the Act provides that a lawyer who has applied to renew their practising certificate may continue to practise while the application is being considered. This may include cases where proceedings are ongoing."

Asked if a lawyer could be suspended pending a complaint, the spokesperson said only the tribunal could make an order that a lawyer be suspended from practice, including for an interim period while any disciplinary process is underway, or strike a lawyer off the roll of barristers and solicitors following referral from a Standards Committee.

The Disciplinary Tribunal is administered by the Ministry of Justice.

Asked why the register did not have the expiry date for the lawyer's practising certificate, the spokesperson said the Society was unable to comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

"Speaking generally, practising certificates have an expiry date of 30 June each year."

Ministry of Justice acting group manager of National Service Delivery Louisa Carroll said the Ministry could not comment on the circumstances of any individual lawyer or active court proceedings.

Asked about the lawyer receiving legal aid clients, Carroll said legal aid providers must meet and maintain approval requirements and comply with the Legal Services Act, their legal aid provider contract, and professional obligations.

"Legal aid providers are also required to notify the Ministry within five working days if they are charged with, or convicted of, an offence punishable by imprisonment."

"Where the Ministry becomes aware of concerns about a provider, it may consider those concerns through its complaints, audit, quality assurance and provider approval processes."

Carroll said depending on the circumstances, the Ministry may take a range of actions, including imposing restrictions on a provider, modifying or cancelling their approval to undertake legal aid work, or referring matters to the New Zealand Law Society.

"Approved providers remain eligible to receive legal aid assignments unless their approval is changed, restricted, suspended, or cancelled.

World.title: Healthline calls in reinforcements amid biggest flu outbreak in 10 years
World.content:
Healthline calls in reinforcements for flu surge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Healthline has called in reinforcements to cope with a deluge of calls amid the biggest flu outbreak in years.

Flu-related hospitalisations are at a 10-year high in Auckland, with national infection rates at a four-year high and rising.

Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley earlier said the entire health system was under pressure, with the spike being driven by influenza A along with cases of RSV, cold viruses and some Covid-19 cases.

The chief operating officer of Wakarongorau Aotearoa, which operates Healthline, Brian O'connell, told Checkpoint the service was handling about 20 percent more calls in the past seven days compared to July.

He said a normal day would see about 1000 calls but this was now up to 1200 to 1300 a day.

Healthline had increased resourcing by about 10 percent, he said. This meant at any time there were about 25 nurses and paramedics on and the current wait time was 10 minutes.

"When people are calling Healthline they're connected with one of our nurses or paramedics and can talk through concerns and then our team will work with them about how urgently they need to seek health advice or give advice to keep themselves well at home."

Out of every five people Healthline spoke to, O'connell said only one would be diverted through to hospital or calling 111.

He said Healthline could be especially helpful at the moment for any parent who was worried about a sick child.

"Speaking to our clincial team can really help give you that reassurance and make sure you're not going to the wrong place."

About 30 percent of the calls Healthline received were for children under the age of 5.

As a result, O'connell said Plunket had been helping out by putting on more nurses who could take calls relating to young children.

Plunket told Checkpoint in a statement, it was taking an extra 200 calls a day as it helped to support Healthline with addressing demand.

It said some whānau might experience longer wait times than usual.

How can the flu outbreak be addressed?

Should people be masking up as flu outbreaks surge? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

University of Otago professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker told Checkpoint, more needed to be done sooner in the future, including stronger advice about masks.

"The problem is when we're at this stage of the epidemic curve we've left it too late because we're already overwhelming the health system. It's hard to change the trajectory."

Professor of Public Health Dr Michael Baker. (File photo) Supplied / Department of Public Health

He said a graded response to dampen down transmission would be a good idea along with continuing with vaccination.

"But now we're stuck in this situation and I hope we can do better in future.

Winter respiratory infections usually went from May to October, Baker said, with the intensity varying greatly year-to-year.

Baker said we needed to get better at rapidly ramping up control measures including mask use in enclosed environments and additional precautions in high risk settings like public transport and waiting rooms.

Employers could also get more active at discouraging workers from coming to work sick, he said, and encourage working from home.

There were also additional RAT tests available now that could test for influenza, RSV and Covid-19, Baker said, which were tools available to be used in strategic ways.

"Some countries do have systems for communicating the level of respiratory risk in the community. We don't have a graded system in place to know when to issue those warnings - a system like this needs a bit of design work, working with community groups, Māori and those that are particularly vulnerable to get a sense of the kinds of warnings they would appreciate.

"We've published work in the past about having a graded system on this for seasonal infections...it's quite a well established approach but we do need that willingness from our political and health leaders."

World.title: Report on Mt Maunganui landslide risk unread: Tauranga City Council
World.content:
Tauranga councillors had report outlining landslide risk Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tauranga councillors had a detailed report showing there was a high risk people could die if their local campground got hit by a landslide but no one read the report.

The council said that despite the report being in an August 2025 council agenda, it was not read and the meeting never happened.

Five months after the meeting was cancelled, six people were killed in a landslide as debris came off Mount Maunganui and covered a large area of the campground.

Retired High Court Justice Paul Davison KC found information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded and then left.

But on Wednesday, when his report was released, council chief executive Marty Grenfell told RNZ that no senior staff saw those reports.

"These reports were never escalated to a point where anybody at a senior level within the organisation could provide guidance, direction, and ensure that they were appropriately managed."

Grenfell said the reports stayed at "operational level".

"Our systems were such that from an organisation perspective, we weren't aware that these reports were being commissioned."

However, the council's own website showed that a June 2025 geo hazard report was included in an August agenda.

It says the rock stability monitoring report was sent out along with the meeting agenda, but the meeting was cancelled so none of the councillors actually read it.

The chief executive's name is on the agenda's cover, but in a statement the council said this did not mean he read the information either.

A council spokesperson said the report itself cost more than $12,000. They said the meeting was cancelled because of concerns about the number of councillors able to attend, but they were not sure why it was never rescheduled.

Call for accountability

Local group Lobby for Good spokesperson Erika Harvey said it was even more concerning that the information was circulated but never read.

"How do you think the families feel now? Now, not only did they know, not only could they have prevented it, but actually nobody actually cared to read it.

"You cannot tell me that this is just something that you should say, oh well, we'll learn next time from this. This is worse than a systemic failure. This is a governance failure. This is, in my opinion, this is negligence.

"If no one's reading anything and you can just use that as an excuse not to know what's going on, when you're paid more than the Prime Minister - over $600,000 Marty gets paid, more than the Prime Minister - to run a town, a city. Could you imagine if the Prime Minister said that? Oh sorry, we didn't know. I didn't get the report and six people died."

She said she had lost faith in the system and that someone needed to be held accountable.

"Now there's a document that says it could have been prevented, along with a report, and here's how much it could have been prevented but now nobody read it."

Echoes of CTV collapse

It brought back memories for a man whose wife died in the collapse of the CTV building during the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.

Maan Alkaisi from the CTV Families Group said they also waited for answers, accountability and justice but that the councillors failing to read their own report was proof that local government was not learning from previous failings.

"That really of course resonates with what happened with the CTV, because there were two reports explicitly highlighting a risk of collapse in case of earthquake and yet no action was taken."

He said it was disappointing and concerning that after 15 years nothing appeared to have changed.

"The whole idea from all these investigations, royal commissions, and police and ... WorkSafe and all that - they conduct investigations and they make recommendations and then none of these recommendations [have] actually been followed up or implemented, and we risk more people and more people lose their lives, and we know that this is preventable.

World.title: Third case of H5 bird flu found in Wellington region
World.content:
A third case of H5 bird flu has been detected in a northern giant petrel, in the Wairarapa.

Ministry for Primary Industries says it was found dead on a remote Cape Palliser beach.

It follows cases found in a kāhu, or swamp harrier, and a brown skua.

It was found by a Department of Conservation (DOC) ranger, who notified the MPI hotline.

Samples received by the MPI Animal Health Laboratory on 14 August were tested and initially found low levels of influenza virus in the bird. It took several rounds of testing to confirm bird flu.

MPI chief veterinary officer Mary van Andel said this latest case had not come as a shock.

"Although it's disappointing to find one of these infected birds, it's really not surprising.

"We can definitely expect to have more of these ocean-going seabirds arrive in New Zealand. We know that they come here. We know that birds in the Southern Ocean are infected with clade 2.3.4.4b."

Dr van Andel said chicken and eggs were absolutely safe to eat and there were no food safety concerns.

"This is a single detection in an ocean-going seabird, so no spread in New Zealand wildlife detected, no detections in poultry in New Zealand, and so really not much has changed."

She asked people to report any sightings of sick or dead birds to MPI.

"What we need is for people who see groups of sick or dying birds to report those.

World.title: Brisbane boys go back to back with stunning come-from-behind wins
World.content:
Brisbane has mounted a stunning second-half fightback to deny Josh Papali'i a win in his final game at Canberra Stadium before the Dolphins shook off another slow start to take down the Eels.

The loss ended the Raiders' faint finals hopes after they looked on track for a celebratory victory while leading 30-16 with 18 minutes left in the retiring Papali'i's hometown farewell.

But 18 straight points, capped saw the Broncos to a 34-30 win in scenes reminiscent of their comeback win at the same ground in last year's finals series, albeit in much lower stakes and far more conventional fashion.

At Lang Park, the Dolphins consolidated their place in the league's top four with a 34-16 win over the Eels after they too trailed 10-0 after just 20 minutes.

The Dolphins have made a habit of relying on their sparkling attack to fire them back from slow starts, and it has now carried them to five straight wins and four points clear of Cronulla in fourth spot.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: Australia names team for second Test against Bangladesh
World.content:
Australia have resisted the temptation to play four specialist fast bowlers against Bangladesh in the second Test in Mackay, as captain Pat Cummins confirmed Matt Renshaw would open the batting.

The recalled Renshaw is a straight swap for Jake Weatherald, who was dropped after six underwhelming Test matches.

The pitch at Great Barrier Reef Arena is expected to assist the pacemen, but off spinner Nathan Lyon, after taking 1-102 in the first innings of the nine-wicket loss by Australia in Darwin, will play his 143rd Test.

Australia vs Bangladesh second Test preview Winter cricket continues in the Top End, with Australia looking for a big response in the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay.

Outstanding paceman Scott Boland did not play in Darwin and will now have to wait until the tour of South Africa in October for his next Test, after starring in last summer's Ashes.

Pitch curator Peter Kazakoff said the Mackay wicket would suit fast bowlers on both sides.

"That is what we are aiming for, a lot of pace," he said.

"We want the ball to come through really nicely. We have got the same sort of clay as the Gabba, so we are expecting similar sort of characteristics to that."

Australia confirmed their side, with Lyon in it, an hour after captain Cummins held a press conference where he said he was considering an all-out pace attack.

Kazakoff said there would be a role for Lyon and the Bangladesh spinners.

"I think the spinners will come into the game, going off previous first-class games here," he said.

"Spinners have had a big say later in the match. Obviously those first-class games were a bit later in the year when it was a bit warmer.

"It is a lot cooler this time of year. The moisture will come out of the wicket less and slower."

There has been a lot of talk about "soul-searching" in the Australian camp after the Darwin loss, but Cummins said he was confident of a response.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"In home Test matches we pride ourselves on winning as many as we can," he said.

"It's funny. I think if we played really well and we lost you'd feel like we needed to do some soul-searching.

"I certainly felt like we didn't play anywhere near our best and they played really well. When we play well, fortunately we have got a decent body of work to look back on."

Weatherald's axing was simple to explain for Cummins, who said he was "awesome around the group" but did not deliver.

"Over the course of six Test matches he didn't quite score the runs he or we would have liked," Cummins said.

Renshaw, 30, will play his first Test in three years after averaging 49.9 in Sheffield Shield cricket last summer, including scoring three centuries.

"[Renshaw] has been really impressive and had some great off-season tours of Pakistan and Bangladesh recently with white-ball (formats). He looks in good nick," Cummins said.

"He had a really good Shield season last season.

"Some of the kind of chat about [Renshaw] in the past is that he can look different from day to day.

"When you get to the back half of your career as a batter you want to really know what you look like at your best, and I think he does that.

"I hope he brings his best version every day, is nice and sharp and puts the pressure on the bowlers."

Australia XI for second Test: Matthew Renshaw, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood

AAP

World.title: Swans AFLW captain and coach say club is 'united' amid scandal
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy has said her players have had "open conversations" in the wake of the scandal that has engulfed her club and led to five men's players being suspended for the rest of the season.

McEvoy, along with AFLW coach Colin O'Riordan, spoke to the media on Friday afternoon, saying the women's program supports the sanctions imposed on Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. The press conference has ended AFLW players would like to have say in whether five suspended men's players return Lucy McEvoy is asked if the AFLW players have discussed whether they want the five suspended players to return to the club. She tells the media that conversation has not happened but, when the time comes, the AFLW players would like to be part of the discussion. 'Moment for all women to stand together', McEvoy Here is more from Lucy McEvoy, speaking about the wider issue at the heart of this week's scandal. "There's no doubt, I think, a lot of women in the community are all feeling the same. "It's obviously an issue within the community that needs to be addressed, and I think this week it has been. "I applaud the club in the way they have handled it, and respected us as a women's program. "I think it's an important moment for all women to stand together and understand that all women deserve respect." Show more

Those five players will miss the remainder of the AFL season following club-imposed suspensions for breaking team standards in Melbourne earlier this week.

Victoria Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation, where it is alleged one player touched a woman without her consent. No charges have been laid, and no-one has been formally interviewed.

Speaking on Friday, McEvoy said the AFLW program supported the club-imposed suspensions to the five men's players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

"On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down," McEvoy said.

"To the players, we are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people were.

"We know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club."

McEvoy said it had been a big week for the women's program, who will face Essendon at the Sydney Cricket Ground this weekend.

The Swans were hoping to celebrate this week's double-header with the men's round 24 clash with North Melbourne following the AFLW match on Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of this week's scandal, McEvoy said members of the women's program were processing their emotions and the situation.

"We've had some really open conversations as a group this week, and with the club more broadly," she said.

"We've felt the support both internally and externally as well.

"The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves."

When asked how this week has affected the reputation of the Sydney Swans, McEvoy said the club, both men's and women's teams, must work to regain the public's trust.

"There's no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit," she said.

"We will do whatever we can as a club, both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans, and the community more broadly."

O'Riordan, who played 34 AFL matches for the Swans between 2015 and 2022 before becoming the club's AFLW coach this season, said he was disappointed that he had to address this scandal.

"The actions of a small number of people have impacted a lot of people, especially the women in our football club and wider community," he said.

"As a man who was brought up with strong morals and a strong sense of what is right and wrong, [it's] disappointing to be standing here today and be talking about something like this.

"Growing up, I was always taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life.

"That is especially important in how you treat women."

O'Riordan said the club had remained "incredibly united" in the wake of the scandal.

"This is a united club. It always has been and always will be," he said.

World.title: Panthers NRL finals charge dealt blow by Cogger's three-match ban
World.content:
Penrith is in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart.

Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals.

Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole.

Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning The Penrith Panthers hold on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers' 22-14 win on Thursday night.

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney's Ashton Ward.

If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Cogger also received a $3,000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash.

But the 29-year-old's suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish.

Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers' starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith's comeback victory in the 2023 grand final.

But Cogger's illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week's clash with Canterbury.

AAP

World.title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have denied there is a rift in their playing group as they addressed the ongoing scandal engulfing the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not say whether other staff members or players were present, as the club denied comments suggesting more men from the Swans were present in the room.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about what happened in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown.

"Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened," he said.

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit".

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We're going to work as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more

Both Cox and Mills apologised to the club's AFLW team, with Mills saying he had addressed the group personally.

"I acknowledged their pain, and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group," he said.

Cox added that he hoped the supporters would still come out in force for the double-header at the SCG this weekend.

"I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs," he said.

"We want to show that on Sunday."

Sydney's men's team rounds out its home and away season with a clash against North Melbourne on Sunday afternoon at the SCG, a match preceded by an AFLW match between Sydney's women's team and Essendon's women's team at the same venue.

World.title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
World.content:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

World.title: Test history looms, Renshaw returns as Australia and Bangladesh go again
World.content:
Australia was handed an historic, humbling nine-wicket defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin earlier this week.

It was the first time the Tigers had claimed a Test-match victory in Australia, and will have prompted some serious soul searching for the hosts, who were comprehensively second-best against the world's ninth ranked team.

Tomorrow morning, more history will be made, with Mackay's Harrup Park becoming the 12th Australian venue to host a Test when the teams begin the second and final match of the series.

You can listen to live coverage of the Test on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog

What needs to change for Mackay?: ABC Cricket Podcast

Australia has made one change to its squad for the encounter, with Matt Renshaw coming in for Jake Weatherald, while the return of an exciting young quick sees Bangladesh faced with a selection dilemma.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does the second Test begin?

The second Test between Australia and Bangladesh gets underway on Saturday August 22, with the first session of play beginning at 10am AEST in Mackay, QLD.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 9:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory (ACST), and 8am in Western Australia (AWST).

These are the session times for the five scheduled days of cricket:

First: 10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST)

10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST) Second: 12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST)

12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST) Third: 3:00pm – 5:00pm AEST (2:30pm — 4:30pm ACST, 1:00pm — 3:00pm AWST)

And an extra half hour of play will almost certainly be tacked on to the end of each day in an attempt to bowl the full compliment of overs.

Background on Australia's newest Test venue

The Great Barrier Reef Arena will become the 12th venue to host a men's Test in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Mackay's Harrup Park, also known as the Great Barrier Reef Arena, is set to become Australia's 12th Test venue, the first addition to the list since Canberra's Manuka Oval hosted its debut match in 2019.

The venue has hosted just two Sheffield Shield matches and a pair of Australia A fixtures in the past decade, so it is a relatively unknown quantity when it comes to professional red ball cricket.

But it has seen international action in the past, with both Australia's women's and men's teams playing white-ball games there, and the ground held a youth Test between Australia and India last year.

The most recent Shield match at the venue came in October 2023, when, off the back off a mammoth first dig of 9-501d, Queensland completed an innings victory over Victoria.

Renshaw, in-line to play his first Test in three years tomorrow, was the player-of-the-match in that game, scoring 135 to become the only player to hit two First Class centuries at the venue.

Who is playing?

Renshaw returns to the Australian team after a three-year absence. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Australia has made one change to its squad since the first Test, with opening batter Renshaw coming into the playing group at the expense of Weatherald.

Weatherald returned scores of 23 and 0 in front of his home crowd in Darwin, following on from a disappointing debut series against England last summer.

Renshaw comes into the squad as what appears to be a straight swap, with the Queenslander having scored three Shield centuries at the top of the order last season, averaging 49.90.

However, the last of Renshaw's 14 Tests came in the middle order in Delhi three and a half years ago.

Josh Inglis, the only other batter in the squad not to have played in Darwin, is also in the mix for a return to the team, with Marnus Labuschagne continuing to skate on thin ice at No. 3 after scores of 1 and 31 last week.

Cam Green will be looking to push on after his drought-breaking Darwin ton, while Steve Smith will continue his quest for a first-ever Test century against the Tigers.

Scott Boland seems more likely than not to return to the side, with one of the big four of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Nathan Lyon to be rotated.

Cummins missed much of last summer through injury and didn't bowl at all in Bangladesh's second innings in Darwin.

Green scored his first Test century in over two years in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Given Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto labelled his side's victory in the first Test "the biggest win" in the country's cricketing history, it would feel extremely harsh on any of that Bangladeshi XI missing out on selection for tomorrow's match.

But the return to fitness of pace bowler Shoriful Islam has undoubtedly provided the Bangladeshi selectors with food for thought.

Prior to this series, the towering left-arm quick was an unquestioned member of the tourists' best XI, and could come into the side for tweaker Taijul Islam, with all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz proving in Darwin he's more than capable of acting as his side's frontline spinner.

But there will be no return for lightning-fast young seamer Nahid Rana, who has already returned to Bangladesh to continue his recovery from a side strain.

And it appears that Bangladesh could be without Darwin centurion Tanzid Hasan, who didn't bat in training on Thursday due to a neck issue — Soumya Sarkar, who last played Test cricket in 2021 and whose selection for the tour was described as a "a bit of desperation" by chief selector Habibul Bashar, would be Tanzid's likely replacement.

How to watch and follow the Test

ABC Sport will broadcast live radio coverage of the Test via the ABC Cricket button on ABC Listen, plus on ABC Sport Digital Radio around our AFL and NRL coverage.

The commentary team includes former Australia cricketers Jason Gillespie, Phil Jacques and Xavier Doherty, as well as Corbin Middlemas, Jim Maxwell and Ben Cameron.

ABC Sport will also live blog every ball of the Test.

The match will be broadcast on Channel 7 and Foxtel, and streamed on 7Plus and Kayo Sports.

Tech.title: Why does it seem like food recalls are out of control this year?
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Just weeks after Taylor Farms issued a recall of its iceberg lettuce amid a massive cyclospora outbreak, the Food and Drug Administration recalled more than one million eggs that may be contaminated with salmonella. The eggs, which come from Midwest Poultry Services, were distributed to Kroger and smaller grocery stores across the South and Southwest US. Then, Taylor Farms pulled more than a dozen of its products containing jalapeños — including guacamole, salsa, taco dip, and more — from store shelves after its supplier, Coast Citrus Distributors, recalled fresh peppers due to salmonella contamination.

The list of major recalls that occurred over the past few months doesn’t end there, as frozen blueberries and mixed berries sold at Publix stores in multiple states were recalled over concerns about E. coli contamination earlier this month. Some of Outshine’s fruit bars were also removed for potential glass contamination, while even dog food and eye drops have been affected by recent recalls. Altogether, the recent recalls have sickened thousands of people (and some dogs) across the US.

Darin Detwiler, professor emeritus at Northeastern and adjunct professor at Michigan State University College of Law, tells The Verge that available data from the FDA suggests that “recall activity has indeed been elevated,” but notes that it’s “too early to know” whether this year’s recalls will outpace the ones issued in 2025.

“This is where recall fatigue can become trust fatigue.”

As of July 31st, we’ve had 122 food and beverage recalls so far this year, compared to 135 during the same period in 2025 and 146 in 2024, according to the Poynter Institute. “We just transitioned through the summer, which for various reasons tends to see more foodborne outbreaks than other months,” Edward Dudley, a professor of food science at Pennsylvania State University, tells The Verge. “There has been an increased effort to highlight these events by media outlets, which is great for public awareness, but doesn’t necessarily reflect a concerning uptick in risk.”

While the current number of recalls may not be significantly higher than previous years, a report from the US Public Interest Research Group notes that we have still seen “a huge increase” in outbreaks of foodborne illnesses. “What we can say is that recall activity in 2026 appears elevated, and some individual recalls are affecting extraordinarily large quantities of food,” Detwiler says. “That distinction matters. A handful of very large recalls can expose far more consumers than dozens of smaller events.” The lettuce-linked cyclospora outbreak contributed to more than 9,000 illnesses in the US, which may make it the third-largest recorded outbreak of foodborne illnesses, according to the PIRG.

Some of these large and small events have been getting a lot of attention. News outlets and television stations have picked up on the recalls published by the FDA and US Department of Agriculture. Online personalities often joined the chorus with their viral recall warning posts racking up thousands of likes and views, bolstered by social media algorithms.

“When recall notices become part of the background noise of everyday life, people may stop paying attention,” Detwiler adds. “Worse, they may begin accepting recalls and outbreaks as simply an unavoidable cost of operating a complex food system… This is where recall fatigue can become trust fatigue.”

The Trump administration’s federal funding cuts may also make it more challenging for agencies to oversee food safety. The FDA’s budget decreased by $271 million compared to last year. It also cut over 4,300 employees in 2025 and 2026, while the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention slashed over 2,800 jobs, as reported by FoodNavigator. In February, the Government Accountability Office said the FDA is currently dealing with staffing shortages as the number of required safety inspections increases.

It also doesn’t help that the CDC pulled back on efforts to track certain foodborne diseases last year, with pathogens like cyclospora, listeria, and shigella no longer included in its surveillance program. The FDA also delayed the deadline to comply with the Traceability Rule, a law that introduces new record-keeping requirements for businesses that manufacture, process, pack, or hold certain kinds of food, including fresh leafy greens, peppers, eggs, tomatoes, and more. The goal of the law is to make it easier to track and remove contaminated food. It was supposed to go into effect in January 2026, but the FDA pushed back its enforcement to 2028.

With fewer federal staff members and looser regulations, efforts to better detect, track, and avoid recalls become more difficult. “The solution is not to communicate less about recalls,” Detwiler adds. “It is to prevent more of them, communicate clearly when they occur, explain what went wrong, strengthen the institutions responsible for detecting hazards, and demonstrate that lessons from previous failures are actually being implemented.”

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 10A is a great deal at 15 percent off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This week, all of Google’s Pixel 11 phones launched, including the $899 Pixel 11, the $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro (with the same processor and starting 12GB RAM as the standard model, but with better cameras), and the $1,899 Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re good phones, but if you don’t mind missing out on their new, exclusive camera and AI features, you can get a great Google-made phone that’s hundreds less.

Google’s Pixel 10A has been sitting at an attractive $424 (originally $499) at Amazon, Best Buy, and at the Google Store since early August, and we’re just highlighting it again here today in case you’re shopping for a phone.

An IP68 rating, 90Hz refresh rate screen, wireless charging, and great design aren’t something you have to pay close to $1,000 to get. Similar to Apple’s iPhone 17E (but with slightly older parts by direct comparison), the Pixel 10A offers many of the same hardware and software features as previous Pixels. Its camera specs and Tensor G4 processor — debuted within the Pixel 9 series — are the biggest differences between the 10A and pricier versions. Our criticism of the 10A focused on how little Google changed compared to the 9A, yet it’s still a good phone if you haven’t upgraded in a while. Read our review.

Tech.title: Major YouTube creators are facing backlash for accepting AI money
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Over the past few days, a number of prominent filmmaking content creators including Matti Haapoja and Sam “Kold” Kolder have posted videos of themselves demonstrating what’s possible with AI platform Higgsfield. The videos highlight Higgsfield’s recently added Seedance 2.5 functionality and pitch these technologies as the future of video production.

In response to these videos, other creators started sharing what appear to be screenshots of partnership offers they’d received from PR firms working on Higgsfield’s behalf. All of this led fans to the conclusion that Higgsfield has been trying to use creators to boost its profile and garner goodwill from the public. Almost immediately, fans began dragging Haapoja and Kolder for seemingly working with Higgsfield. Haapoja’s and Kolder’s videos are not labeled as ads and neither the creators nor Higgsfield responded to The Verge’s questions about whether these were paid partnerships. But in producing and posting videos that feel very much like ads for Higgsfield, both creators left portions of their audiences feeling alienated.

Haapoja and Kolder enthusiastically frame Higgsfield and Seedance 2.5 as innovative tools that have the potential to revolutionize the entertainment industry. Haapoja’s is kind of like an infomercial where he explains how Cully Hill Boys — Higgsfield’s feature-length film starring AI-generated duplicates of YouTubers Mikyle “N3on” Rafiq and Matt Kiatipis — was produced with prompts. Haapoja also demonstrates Seedance 2.5’s capabilities with AI-manipulated footage of himself placed in different sci-fi settings. Kolder’s video — titled “AI is replacing me” — tells a story that starts off with an explanation of Kolder’s background in video production before it becomes a fictionalized, Chappie-esque narrative in which he explores Mauritania with the help of a robot. Both videos blend footage of real people with distinctly uncanny AI-generated imagery.

On Threads, Haapoja’s video was met with pushback from fans and other creators who consider him their peer. Marques Brownlee took issue with Haapoja likening generative AI to the Canon EOS 5D Mark II (an iconic DSLR known for making shooting in 1080p full HD more affordable for independent filmmakers). Brownlee also emphasized that unlike the 5D Mark II (a physical tool people still had to learn how to use), gen AI is “trained on real human-made material without any credit.”

Unlike the overwhelmingly negative feedback to Haapoja’s video, Kolder’s comments section on YouTube was more of a mixed bag, with many viewers responding positively. But for every few “absolute cinema!” or “amazing transitions!” comments, there are people lamenting that “AI defeated our king” and insisting that “no AI can replace creative artists.”

Some of the comments beneath Matti Haapoja’s video about using Higgsfield and Seedance 2.5. Screenshot: The Verge, Threads

The negative reactions to Haapoja’s and Kolder’s videos have been much louder than most of the responses to some of Higgsfield’s other recent creator collaborations. Cully Hill Boys debuted last week without all that much fanfare, which made it seem like viewers might not have had particularly strong feelings either way about it. When you scroll through some of the posts that Cully Hill Boys’ cast shared about the film, there’s a mix of AI boosters cheering Higgsfield on and people knocking the company for being a slop purveyor. For the most part, those criticisms haven’t been aimed at the film’s cast — who gave Higgsfield the right to use their likenesses, but were otherwise not as directly involved in the project’s production as traditional actors would be.

What’s different about Haapoja’s and Kolder’s posts is how they come across as sponsored advertising intended to ingratiate the creators’ audiences with Higgsfield. Even though neither of the creators goes so far as to say “you, too, should absolutely be using these products,” that certainly seems to be the underlying message. The caption for Kolder’s video appears to contain what looks like an affiliate link, offering a 30 percent discount on an annual Higgsfield subscription.

As common as partnerships between brands and creators are today, Haapoja’s and Kolder’s cases show what can happen when people with large social media followings involve themselves with products and companies that don’t align with their audiences’ values. This is a potential issue with basically any product, but by endorsing generative AI in particular, creators are opening themselves up to becoming focal points for people’s negative feelings about the technology. That’s what happened earlier this month when OpenAI invited a gaggle of influencers to a luxury resort in New York for a “Summer Club” retreat. None of those content creators uploaded anything as substantial as lengthy videos showing off OpenAI’s tools, but their posts about the trip and receiving OpenAI-branded swag were more than enough to leave their followers turned off.

While companies like OpenAI and Higgsfield can afford (to some extent) to rub people the wrong way with their s, creators who agree to partnerships with AI companies are in a much more complicated position. Creators can only secure such deals after building large followings, but those followings often consist of people who see them as trustworthy individuals with beliefs similar to their own. For creators like Haapoja and Kolder, whose appeal as filmmakers lies in their own human creativity, this bargain is especially risky. At a time when many AI services and tools are seen as a threat, endorsing the technology can signal to their followers that they aren’t someone to be invested in.

Tech.title: Blue Eye Samurai’s second season will hit Netflix in January
Tech.content:
